title: Routing & Forwarding II Quiz
description: 20 questions covering Distance Vector (RIP), Count-to-Infinity, Split Horizon, Link-State (OSPF), Areas, and BGP Path Vector.

questions.question: Why is Distance Vector routing often characterized as 'Routing by Rumor'?

options.text: Because routers do not know the global network topology; they blindly accept distance claims advertised by immediate neighbors
Because distance vector protocols use unencrypted UDP packets
Because it relies on social network graphs

questions.explanation: Routers in Distance Vector share their whole table with neighbors. A router trusts its neighbor's reported distance without independently verifying the actual path.

questions.question: In RIP (Routing Information Protocol), what is the maximum valid hop count metric, and what value represents 'Infinity' (unreachable)?
questions.explanation: RIP caps networks at 15 hops to mitigate count-to-infinity delays. Metric 16 is defined as unreachable (Infinity).

questions.question: How frequently does a standard RIPv2 router broadcast/multicast its entire routing table to its neighbors?

options.text: Only when an administrator types a command

questions.explanation: RIP sends unsolicited periodic full-table updates every 30 seconds via UDP port 520 (multicast 224.0.0.9 in RIPv2).

questions.question: What causes the 'Count-to-Infinity' problem in Distance Vector routing?

options.text: When a destination link fails, neighbors mutually believe the other still has a path, slowly incrementing the hop count between themselves until reaching 16

questions.explanation: Router B advertises a path that depended on C. When C's link drops, C assumes B has an alternate route and updates its cost. B then updates its cost from C, ping-ponging to 16.

questions.question: What is the core operational rule of the 'Split Horizon' loop prevention mechanism?

options.text: Split routing tables into two halves
Never advertise a route back out the same interface through which it was originally learned

questions.explanation: Split Horizon prevents loops by forbidding a router from advertising a route back to the neighbor that taught it that route in the first place.

questions.question: How does 'Poison Reverse' modify the standard Split Horizon rule?

options.text: Instead of suppressing the advertisement, it explicitly advertises the route back to the source with metric = 16 (Infinity / Poisoned)
It resets the interface MTU to 0

questions.explanation: Poison Reverse actively advertises unreachable (hop 16) back out the ingress interface, eliminating race conditions in multi-router topologies.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'Hold-Down Timer' in distance vector routing?

options.text: To pause packet transmission when CPU temperature rises
When a route is marked down, the router ignores any new updates for that route for a stabilization window (e.g. 180s) to allow loop flushes
To keep the interface link up during cable unplugging
To synchronize router clocks with UTC

questions.explanation: Hold-down timers prevent premature acceptance of stale or looping route claims while the network topology is still stabilizing.

questions.question: What is a 'Triggered Update' (Flash Update) in distance vector protocols?

options.text: An update sent immediately when a route metric changes, without waiting for the 30-second timer to expire
An update triggered by an email alert
A packet sent to wake up sleeping routers

questions.explanation: Triggered updates accelerate convergence by broadcasting link failures the exact microsecond they occur.

questions.question: How does Link-State routing (OSPF) fundamentally differ from Distance Vector routing?

options.text: Link-state routers exchange entire routing tables; distance vector routers exchange single packets
Every link-state router floods local Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) so all routers build an identical Link-State Database (LSDB), then run Dijkstra independently
Link-state protocols only work on Wi-Fi
Distance vector uses Dijkstra; link-state uses Bellman-Ford

questions.explanation: Link-state routers have complete visibility of the entire topological map (LSDB) and independently compute their own shortest-path tree using Dijkstra.

questions.question: Which of the following are standard OSPF packet types? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.explanation: OSPF defines 5 packet types: Hello, DBD, LSR, LSU, and LSAck (Type 5).

questions.question: What transport layer protocol does OSPF use to carry its control packets across intermediate links?

options.text: Raw IP directly using Protocol Number 89

questions.explanation: OSPF does not use TCP or UDP. It encapsulates packets directly in raw IPv4/IPv6 packets with IP Protocol Number 89.

questions.question: What is the mandatory central area in a hierarchical OSPF deployment to which all other areas must connect?
questions.explanation: Area 0 (0.0.0.0) is the core Backbone Area. All inter-area traffic must transit through Area 0 to prevent routing loops.

questions.question: What is the role of an Area Border Router (ABR) in OSPF?

options.text: A router that connects to external non-OSPF networks like BGP
A router with interfaces in Area 0 and one or more standard areas, summarizing routes and confining SPF recalculations
A router that operates as a DNS caching resolver
A router that only forwards multicast traffic

questions.explanation: ABRs connect Area 0 to sub-areas. They summarize internal area topology into summary LSAs, preventing link flaps in one area from triggering SPF runs in other areas.

questions.question: On a broadcast multi-access Ethernet network with N = 10 OSPF routers, how many adjacencies would form without DR/BDR election?
questions.explanation: Full mesh peering requires N(N-1)/2 adjacencies. For 10 routers, that is 10*9/2 = 45 redundant adjacencies flooding duplicate LSAs.

questions.question: How does the election of a Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) solve this scalability bottleneck?

options.text: It turns off 8 of the 10 routers
Routers form adjacencies ONLY with the DR and BDR (multicast 224.0.0.6), reducing adjacencies from O(N^2) to O(N)
It switches from OSPF to RIP

questions.explanation: All other routers (DROthers) peer only with the DR/BDR, reducing total adjacencies to 2N - 3, dramatically conserving CPU and link bandwidth.

questions.question: What is an Autonomous System (AS) in the context of global internet routing?

options.text: A collection of connected IP routing networks controlled by a single administrative entity with a unified routing policy (e.g. AS15169 for Google)
An artificial intelligence model that manages routers

questions.explanation: An Autonomous System (AS) is an administrative domain (e.g. ISP, university, tech giant) identified by a globally unique Autonomous System Number (ASN).

questions.question: What protocol is the de facto standard Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) routing the global internet between different Autonomous Systems?
questions.explanation: BGP-4 is the glue of the internet, exchanging reachability and policy paths between thousands of global Autonomous Systems.

questions.question: Why is BGP classified as a 'Path Vector' protocol rather than pure Distance Vector or Link State?

options.text: Because it routes vectors of floating point numbers
Because it advertises the complete sequence of Autonomous System Numbers (AS_PATH) traversed to reach each destination prefix
Because it uses vector graphics for network maps

questions.explanation: Instead of advertising pure hop counts, BGP includes the entire path of ASNs in the AS_PATH attribute.

questions.question: How does BGP's AS_PATH attribute provide immediate, foolproof routing loop detection without running Dijkstra's algorithm?

options.text: If a border router receives a BGP advertisement containing its own Autonomous System Number in the AS_PATH, it immediately discards the route
It checks if the AS_PATH has more than 16 hops
It pings all ASNs in the path
It computes a CRC-32 on the ASNs

questions.explanation: If a router sees its own ASN in the AS_PATH, it knows the route has already passed through its network, so accepting it would create an inter-domain loop. It drops it instantly.

questions.question: What transport layer protocol and port number does BGP use to establish reliable peer sessions?
questions.explanation: BGP relies on TCP Port 179 for point-to-point connection establishment, retransmission, and reliability.
